title: An Equity Lens for Ordinary Decisions
before: A conversation about six questions for ordinary decisions: purpose, participation, requirements, access, evidence and consequences.

turns.text: An Equity Lens for Ordinary Decisions focuses on choices we make all the time: shortening a notice, setting a deadline, deciding who gets an invitation. This course offers six questions about purpose, participation, requirements, access, evidence and consequences, so we can look at an ordinary decision carefully before treating it as settled.

The opening case asks a sharp question: efficient for whom? Removing an explanation from a notice may shorten staff work while leaving readers to find the information somewhere else. So what does the change make easier, and who now has to do more? The course asks us to consider the reader’s task before accepting “simpler” as a complete explanation.

That’s the core of the lens. It examines who can participate, what requirements serve, whose experience is relevant, and how benefits and burdens may differ. It connects evidence with alternatives and a considered next step. And the course is careful to say that a question isn’t yet a finding, and a practice draft isn’t formal approval.

The first practice situation develops the opening case. A notice drops the description of how to submit a supporting document because staff expect readers to know the route. A comparison table shows how the work shifts between staff and readers. Then you’ll choose a response, and one option removes the document requirement without checking its source.

Purpose is a useful place to start. Ask what a requirement is meant to achieve and what actual source supports it. A familiar practice might be required, or useful, or simply carried forward without examination. The course also cautions against calling every effort a barrier. The aim is to explain the relevant purpose and effect, not to assume one.

It also asks us to name people carefully. “Everyone benefits” doesn’t explain whose experience was considered. Who encounters the step, and who may never reach it? At the same time, we shouldn’t predict an individual from a group label or build an unnecessary identity inventory. Participation matters, too, because people affected by a change can identify consequences staff might miss.

The workplace case is about a development opportunity offered only to employees able to travel the next day. Availability may reflect scheduling, access or resources rather than the capability the training is meant to build. You’ll practice examining what that condition serves. One of the options swings the other way, promising an arrangement without checking whether it’s available.

Then the course turns to policy. A proposed rule can change documentation, timing, access or responsibilities before its effects are understood. In the practice case, a proposal adds an online confirmation step, and a community participant explains that the current route is already hard to use. The course treats that account as a reason for a focused question, not a complete impact finding.

Evidence runs through all of it. Numbers can describe a recorded pattern, while accounts reveal how a step is experienced, and missing information is unknown rather than reassuring. The familiar option needs evidence too, and an alternative may simply move the barrier somewhere else. Recommendations should match the scope the evidence supports and keep decision responsibilities visible.

For the writing activity, you’ll draft a small equity inquiry using the notice, the training invitation or the policy proposal. You’ll name the purpose, one possible burden, an affected perspective, and the evidence needed to examine it. Then you’ll propose a fitting next question without claiming the issue is decided. The course also reminds us to keep asking after a change is made.

As you go, think of one ordinary decision in your own work this month, perhaps a template, a deadline or an invitation list. Which of the six questions have you already asked about it, and which one is still open? Bring that decision with you. The lens is most useful where the work actually takes shape.

guidance.title: A question, not a finding
guidance.text: The equity lens is a set of questions, not a verdict. Asking whether a step shifts work onto readers does not mean it does. It means the effect is worth examining with evidence, alternatives and the people who encounter the step. Keeping that difference clear helps colleagues engage with the question, and it keeps formal approval with the people responsible for it.

guidance.title: After the change
guidance.text: Think of a change your team made recently, such as a revised form or a new step. What evidence do you have that it serves the intended task? A reviewed draft, an implemented change and an improved experience are different things. Which of those can you speak to, and what would you still need to learn from the people who use it?
